Who I Am

I am David P. Adekunle — a Nigerian geographer, research and education writer, and author. My work sits at the intersection of place, people, and policy, drawing from the rich and complex landscape of Nigerian society to produce writing that informs, challenges, and inspires.

Geography, for me, is not merely a discipline — it is a lens through which I read the world. Every map tells a story. Every spatial pattern reflects a decision, a history, a power structure. My goal is to translate these stories into accessible, rigorous, and meaningful narratives.

What Drives Me

Nigeria is one of the most geographically, demographically, and culturally complex nations on earth. Yet it is too often reduced in academic and public discourse to its problems. I believe in writing that restores complexity, honours nuance, and demands better from our institutions.

Education is at the heart of my research interests — not just schooling, but the broader question of how knowledge is produced, distributed, and denied in Nigerian society. Who gets to learn? Who gets to write? Who gets to be heard?

My Background

My academic and professional background is rooted in geography and the social sciences. I have developed expertise in research methodology, spatial analysis, GIS mapping, academic writing, and education commentary. I am equally comfortable in the field, in the library, or at the keyboard — translating data into insight and insight into impact.

Long-Term Vision

"To become one of Nigeria's foremost geographic voices — a researcher, writer, and author whose work shapes how Nigeria understands itself and how the world understands Nigeria."

EnvironmentMay 14, 2026

Cross River's Flooding Crisis: What Geography Tells Us That Politics Won't

By David P. Adekunle  ·  Geographic Commentary  ·  May 14, 2026

Every year, the floods return to Cross River State, triggering alarms, press briefings, and renewed appeals for federal intervention. And then, when the waters recede, so does the urgency — until the next rainy season arrives and the cycle begins again.

This week, Governor Bassey Otu received the Director-General of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) in Calabar as part of the 2026 National Flood Preparedness and Awareness Campaign. He described flooding as "a painful and persistent challenge" and called for coordinated action from all levels of government. NEMA confirmed that Cross River is among Nigeria's highest flood-risk states this year, with vulnerable communities stretching across Abi, Akamkpa, Calabar Municipality, Etung, Ikom, Obubra, and beyond.

These are the right conversations to have. But they are happening too late, too reactively, and without sufficient geographic grounding.

A Geographic Condition, Not an Accident

The fact is, Cross River State is not flooding by accident. It sits in Nigeria's humid tropical rainforest belt — one of the wettest regions in West Africa. The Cross River itself is a major drainage system fed by rainfall from Cameroon's highlands. The state's terrain includes low-lying floodplains, poorly drained coastal soils, and riverine communities built on land that water has always claimed seasonally.

This is not a crisis that arrived without warning. It is a geographic condition that was always present — and that decades of inadequate spatial planning have turned into a recurring disaster.

When colonial and post-colonial authorities established settlements, roads, and critical infrastructure in Cross River State without proper flood-risk planning, they laid the foundation for the crises being witnessed today. Likewise, drainage systems built for far lower rainfall levels — long before climate change intensified precipitation patterns — were bound to become inadequate over time.

Geography does not cause these floods alone; it sets the stage. And ignoring it guarantees that each intervention will be temporary.

The Incomplete Infrastructure Problem

Perhaps the most troubling geographical insight from this week's reports was Governor Otu's reference to abandoned and unfinished drainage and water channel projects. It reflects a familiar Nigerian pattern — infrastructure projects initiated with fanfare but left incomplete, drainage networks that suddenly terminate within communities because funding dried up or political leadership changed midway through execution.

Incomplete drainage is in some ways worse than no drainage at all. It redirects water unpredictably, concentrating flood impact on communities that were not originally at risk. It is a man-made amplifier of a natural hazard.

A comprehensive geographic assessment of flood-control infrastructure across Cross River State — identifying what was proposed, what was completed, what was abandoned, and which communities remain vulnerable — would reveal a deeply troubling reality. More importantly, it would provide a clear roadmap for where urgent intervention is most needed.

Floods and the Education Crisis

It is important to recognise that the impact of recurring floods extends far beyond destroyed homes and flooded farmlands. The effects ripple through entire communities. Families forced to relocate, whether temporarily or permanently, often interrupt their children's education. Schools in low-lying areas are damaged, occupied by displaced persons, or rendered inaccessible, leading to prolonged disruptions in learning. Girls, whose access to education is already more fragile in many rural communities, are especially vulnerable to dropping out during and after flood disasters.

In a state where educational performance in several rural local government areas already falls below much of southern Nigeria's average, seasonal flooding cannot be separated from the broader education crisis. They are interconnected challenges, manifesting in different forms at different times.

Planning, Not Just Preparedness

The flood preparedness campaigns by NEMA remain important. Early warning systems save lives, and public sensitisation plays a critical role in reducing vulnerability. Yet preparedness alone, without long-term structural planning, amounts to managing the consequences while neglecting the root causes.

What Nigeria urgently requires is legally enforceable flood-risk zoning, drainage master plans grounded in hydrological and environmental data rather than political expediency, and development control agencies empowered to prevent construction on floodplains. Beyond that, the country needs continuity in infrastructure delivery — not projects celebrated at groundbreaking ceremonies only to be abandoned midway.

The flooding in Cross River State is neither unpredictable nor mysterious. The rivers have followed these paths for generations, and the rains do not arrive without warning. What has consistently failed is the commitment to plan in harmony with the geography instead of in defiance of it.

Governor Otu is justified in drawing attention to the crisis. However, alarms without spatial planning, accurate mapping, and the political resolve to complete critical infrastructure achieve little beyond echoing above rising floodwaters.

The land remembers what the politicians forget.
David P. Adekunle is a geographer and development commentator. This piece is part of an ongoing series on environment, planning, and spatial justice in Nigeria.

EducationMay 2026

The State of Education in Nigeria: A Geographic Perspective

Nigeria's education crisis is not just a funding problem — it is a spatial problem. Schools are not distributed equally across the country, and the gap between urban and rural access tells a story that statistics alone cannot capture.

The Spatial Divide

When we map school distribution across Nigeria's 36 states, a stark pattern emerges. The South-West, particularly Lagos and Ogun states, enjoys significantly higher school density than the North-East or North-West. This is not merely a reflection of population distribution — it reflects decades of differential investment, colonial legacy, and political neglect.

Beyond Enrollment Numbers

Federal government data often cites enrollment figures as evidence of educational progress. But enrollment is not education. A child enrolled in a school with no furniture, no textbooks, and an absent teacher is not receiving an education — they are occupying a building that qualifies as a school on paper.

What Geography Tells Us

Geographic analysis of educational outcomes reveals something important: the farther you are from an urban centre in Nigeria, the lower your educational attainment is likely to be. This is true controlling for income, ethnicity, and religion. Space itself — distance, terrain, infrastructure — is an independent variable in educational inequality.

This has profound implications for policy. Education reform that does not account for geography is education reform that will fail the children who need it most.

Urban GeographyMay 2026

Youth Unemployment and the Geography of Opportunity in Nigeria

Where you are born in Nigeria largely determines what opportunities are available to you. The concentration of economic activity in Lagos and Abuja, while vast regions remain underserved, is not an accident — it is a policy outcome.

A Tale of Two Nigerias

Nigeria's youth unemployment rate hovers above 40% by most credible estimates. But this national figure obscures a geographic reality: youth in rural areas and in the North face unemployment rates that dwarf even this sobering average.

The Infrastructure Connection

Opportunity follows infrastructure. Roads, electricity, internet connectivity, financial services — these are the foundations on which economic activity is built. Their uneven distribution across Nigerian space is perhaps the most consequential geographic fact of contemporary Nigerian life.

Addressing youth unemployment without addressing the spatial concentration of infrastructure is addressing symptoms while leaving the disease untouched.

DevelopmentApril 2026

Housing Crisis in Nigerian Cities: Who Is Building for Whom?

The Nigerian housing market is one of the most glaring examples of spatial injustice in contemporary Africa. As luxury estates multiply in Lekki and Maitama, millions remain in informal settlements with no security of tenure.

The Numbers

Nigeria has a housing deficit estimated at 28 million units. This number has grown steadily over the past two decades despite — or perhaps because of — various government housing schemes. The question is not whether Nigeria is building, but who it is building for.

Informal Settlements as Geography

Informal settlements are not planning failures — they are planning responses. When formal housing is priced beyond the reach of the majority, people create their own spatial solutions. Ajegunle, Makoko, and hundreds of similar communities across Nigerian cities represent the geographic ingenuity of people systematically excluded from the formal city.

Any serious housing policy must start by recognising this and engaging with informal settlements as legitimate urban space, not problems to be erased.
